q: Organic chemistry is defined as the branch of chemistry that deals with:
o: All compounds that contain carbon, including carbonates
x: Organic chemistry is the study of compounds of carbon with hydrogen (hydrocarbons) and the compounds derived from them. Carbonates, CO and CO₂ contain carbon but are studied as inorganic compounds.

q: A functional group is:
o: The longest chain of carbon atoms in a molecule
A group of compounds differing from each other by CH₂
An atom or group of atoms that gives an organic compound its characteristic properties
The ring of carbon atoms in a cyclic compound
x: A functional group, such as –OH or –COOH, is the reactive part of a molecule that largely decides its chemical properties. A series differing by CH₂ is a homologous series.

q: Which pair of compounds has the same molecular formula but different functional groups?
x: Propanal (aldehyde) and propanone (ketone) are both C₃H₆O. Ethanol and propanol differ by CH₂, ethanoic acid and methyl ethanoate have different formulas, and butane and isobutane have no different functional groups (they differ only in chain).

q: A free radical is best described as:
o: A negative ion carrying a lone pair
A neutral molecule with all electrons paired
An atom or group with an unpaired electron
x: A free radical has an unpaired electron, which makes it very reactive, e.g. Cl• or CH₃•. A positively charged carbon species is a carbocation, not a radical.

q: In almost all organic compounds, each carbon atom forms how many covalent bonds?
x: Carbon has four valence electrons (2s² 2p²) and is tetravalent, forming four covalent bonds in organic compounds, as in CH₄.

q: The functional group of carboxylic acids is:
x: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group, –COOH, as in ethanoic acid CH₃COOH. –CHO is aldehyde, –OH is alcohol and –COOR is ester.

q: Stereoisomers are compounds that have:
o: The same molecular formula but different structural formulas
Different molecular formulas but the same functional group
The same structural formula but different arrangements of atoms in space
The same molecular mass but different elements
x: In stereoisomers the atoms are joined in the same order (same structural formula) but are arranged differently in space. Same molecular formula with different structural formulas describes structural isomers.

q: Free radicals are produced when a covalent bond breaks by:
o: Heterolytic fission, one atom keeping both electrons
Homolytic fission, each atom keeping one electron
Ionisation of the molecule in water
Transfer of a proton to a base
x: In homolytic fission the shared pair splits evenly, so each fragment gets one electron and becomes a radical. Heterolytic fission gives ions (a cation and an anion) instead.

q: The vital force theory was rejected after Wöhler (1828) prepared urea in the laboratory by heating:
x: Wöhler heated ammonium cyanate (NH₄CNO), an inorganic salt, and obtained urea, an organic compound from living things. This showed organic compounds could be made without a living organism.

q: Ethanal (acetaldehyde), CH₃CHO, contains which functional group?
x: The –CHO group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one hydrogen, is the aldehyde group. In a ketone the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon atoms.

q: Which compound shows geometric (cis–trans) isomerism?
x: In but-2-ene each doubly bonded carbon carries two different groups (H and CH₃), so cis and trans forms exist. In the others at least one double-bond carbon carries two identical groups (two H atoms or two CH₃ groups).

q: Saturated hydrocarbons such as methane mainly undergo:
x: Alkanes have only σ bonds and no π bond to add across, so they react by replacing hydrogen atoms with other atoms, e.g. chlorination of methane in sunlight.

q: According to the vital force theory, organic compounds:
o: Could be made only from minerals
Could be made only inside living organisms
Could be made in the laboratory from any element
x: The vital force theory held that a 'vital force' present only in living things was needed to make organic compounds, so they could not be prepared in the laboratory. Wöhler's synthesis of urea disproved it.

q: Propanone (acetone), CH₃COCH₃, belongs to which class of compounds?
x: In CH₃COCH₃ the carbonyl group (C=O) is bonded to two carbon atoms, which makes it a ketone. An aldehyde has the carbonyl at the end of the chain bonded to H.

q: For an alkene to show geometric isomerism, it must have:
o: Free rotation about the C=C bond
A carbon atom attached to four different groups
At least two identical groups on one doubly bonded carbon
Restricted rotation about the C=C bond and two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon
x: The π bond prevents rotation about C=C, and each doubly bonded carbon must carry two different groups so that 'same side' and 'opposite side' arrangements differ. Four different groups on one carbon is the condition for optical isomerism.

q: The typical reactions of alkenes and alkynes are:
x: The loosely held π electrons of a double or triple bond attract electrophiles, and the reagent adds across the multiple bond. Free-radical substitution is typical of alkanes, and nucleophilic substitution of alkyl halides.

q: The ability of carbon atoms to link with one another to form long chains and rings is called:
x: Catenation is self-linking of carbon atoms into chains and rings. It is the main reason for the enormous number of organic compounds; isomerism adds further variety.

q: Methoxymethane (dimethyl ether), CH₃OCH₃, contains which functional group?
x: In CH₃OCH₃ an oxygen atom joins two alkyl groups, the ether linkage R–O–R. It has no O–H bond, so it is not an alcohol, and no C=O, so it is neither ester nor ketone.

q: Which compound does NOT show cis–trans isomerism?
x: In CH₂=CCl₂ one carbon has two H atoms and the other two Cl atoms, so swapping groups gives the same molecule. Each of the other three has two different groups on both doubly bonded carbons.

q: The reaction CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, carried out in diffused sunlight, is an example of:
x: Light splits Cl₂ into chlorine free radicals, which take part in a chain reaction that replaces a hydrogen of methane by chlorine. Two products form, as is typical of substitution.

q: A long-chain alkane is cracked: C₁₄H₃₀ → C₇H₁₆ + X. If X is a single molecule, its formula is:
x: Balance atoms: C 14 − 7 = 7, H 30 − 16 = 14, so X is C₇H₁₄, an alkene (CₙH₂ₙ). Cracking always gives a smaller alkane plus an alkene, so a second C₇H₁₆ cannot balance the hydrogen.

q: Decane is cracked: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₄H₁₀ + 2X, where both molecules of X are the same. X is:
x: After C₄H₁₀ the remaining atoms are C₆H₁₂; shared between two identical molecules this gives C₃H₆, propene. Check: C₃H₆ fits CₙH₂ₙ, an alkene. Propane (C₃H₈) would need 4 more H atoms.

q: Benzene, phenol and naphthalene are obtained mainly from which product of the destructive distillation of coal?
x: Heating coal strongly without air gives coke, coal gas, ammoniacal liquor and coal tar; fractional distillation of the coal tar yields aromatic compounds such as benzene, phenol and naphthalene. Coal gas is mainly H₂ and CH₄.

q: Pyridine, C₅H₅N, has a six-membered ring of five carbon atoms and one nitrogen atom. It is classified as:
x: A ring that contains at least one atom other than carbon (here N) is heterocyclic. Homocyclic or carbocyclic rings, including alicyclic ones, contain only carbon atoms.

q: Catalytic reforming of petroleum fractions is carried out mainly to:
o: Break large molecules into smaller alkenes
Separate petroleum into fractions by boiling point
Convert straight-chain alkanes into branched-chain and aromatic hydrocarbons, raising the octane number
Remove sulphur compounds from crude oil
x: Reforming rearranges molecules (isomerisation, cyclisation, aromatisation) without making them much smaller, giving petrol that knocks less. Breaking big molecules into smaller ones is cracking, the usual mix-up.

q: The IUPAC name of (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂OH is:
x: The longest chain holding the –OH has 4 carbons (butanol). Number from the end nearer the –OH: OH on C-1 and the methyl on C-3, giving 3-methylbutan-1-ol. Numbering from the branch end gives the wrong 2-methylbutan-4-ol.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃COCH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is:
x: The longest chain through the C=O has 5 carbons (pentanone). Numbering from the end nearer the carbonyl puts C=O on C-2 and the methyl on C-3: 3-methylpentan-2-one. Numbering from the other end gives the wrong 4-one.

q: The IUPAC name of HOCH₂CH₂COOH is:
x: –COOH has higher priority than –OH, so the compound is named as an acid and the COOH carbon is C-1; the –OH is then on C-3, written as the prefix hydroxy. 2-Hydroxypropanoic acid is lactic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH, a different compound.

q: The IUPAC name of the ester CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ is:
x: An ester RCOOR′ is named alkyl (R′) first, then the acid part: R′ = ethyl, acid part CH₃COO– = ethanoate. Methyl propanoate (CH₃CH₂COOCH₃) is an isomer, made by reading the groups the wrong way round.

q: Ethylamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂, belongs to which class of compounds?
x: The –NH₂ group joined to an alkyl carbon makes an amine. An amide has –CONH₂, a nitrile –C≡N and a nitro compound –NO₂.

q: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₅H₁₂?
x: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane: 3 chain isomers. Shapes named 3-methylbutane or 2-ethylpropane are only 2-methylbutane drawn another way, so counting them gives 4 or 5.

q: Counting structural isomers only, how many alcohols have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀O?
x: Butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol: 4 alcohols. 7 also counts the three ethers of the same formula, and 5 counts the two mirror-image forms of butan-2-ol.

q: C₂H₅OC₂H₅ and CH₃OCH₂CH₂CH₃ have the same molecular formula and the same functional group but different alkyl groups on either side of it. This type of isomerism is called:
x: Metamerism arises from unequal distribution of carbon atoms on either side of the same functional group, as in these two ethers. Functional group isomers have different groups, e.g. an ether and an alcohol of formula C₄H₁₀O.

q: Which compound contains a chiral carbon atom (one bonded to four different groups)?
x: In lactic acid the central carbon carries H, CH₃, OH and COOH, four different groups, so it shows optical isomerism. In (CH₃)₂CHOH the carbon has two identical CH₃ groups, and the other two have carbons with two H atoms.

q: How many alkenes, including geometric isomers, have the molecular formula C₄H₈?
x: But-1-ene, cis-but-2-ene, trans-but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene: 4. Forgetting the cis–trans pair gives 3, and adding the two ring compounds (cyclobutane, methylcyclopropane), which are not alkenes, gives 6.

q: Which species is an electrophile?
x: An electrophile is electron-deficient and accepts an electron pair; the nitronium ion NO₂⁺ is the electrophile in nitration. NH₃, OH⁻ and H₂O all have lone pairs to donate, so they are nucleophiles.

q: Which carbocation is the most stable?
x: Alkyl groups push electrons towards the positive carbon (+I effect) and spread its charge, so stability is tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl. The tertiary ion (CH₃)₃C⁺ has three such groups.

q: Heterolytic fission of the C–Br bond in (CH₃)₃C–Br gives:
x: In heterolysis the more electronegative atom, Br, keeps both bonding electrons and becomes Br⁻, leaving a tertiary carbocation. Two radicals form only in homolytic fission, and Br⁺ would need the less electronegative carbon to take the pair.

q: Ethene reacts with HBr in the dark, with no peroxide present, to give CH₃CH₂Br. The type of reaction and the change in hybridisation of the two carbon atoms are:
x: H⁺ from HBr attacks the π electrons (electrophilic attack), and Br⁻ then joins the carbocation, so HBr adds across C=C. Each carbon goes from three σ bonds plus a π bond (sp²) to four σ bonds (sp³). Free-radical paths need peroxide or light.

q: In a carbocation such as CH₃⁺, the positively charged carbon atom is:
x: The carbon forms three σ bonds and has no lone pair; its three sp² orbitals lie in a plane at 120° and the empty p orbital is perpendicular. A pyramidal sp³ shape fits the carbanion CH₃⁻, which has a lone pair.
